A Primal-Dual-Assisted Penalty Approach to Bilevel Optimization with Coupled Constraints

Liuyuan Jiang, Quan Xiao, Victor M. Tenorio, Fernando Real-Rojas, Antonio G. Marques, Tianyi Chen

The takeaway

BLOCC combines penalty reformulation with primal-dual information to optimize bilevel problems whose lower-level constraints depend on the upper-level decision.

01Explanation

When an outer decision changes what the inner problem can do

A leader changes the follower’s choices

Consider a network operator deciding which infrastructure to provide. Users then respond within the network that exists. The operator’s decision changes the set of available routes. A bilevel model expresses the sequence, and coupled constraints express the changing feasible set.

The response moves with its boundary

In an ordinary unconstrained inner problem, we can study how an optimum changes through the objective. Here the feasible boundary moves too. A lower-level optimum can sit on an active constraint, so the effect of an outer decision must include both objective and constraint terms.

01

Model the changing feasible set

Represent the follower’s constraints as c(x, y) ≤ 0 rather than using a fixed inner domain.

02

Track primal and dual information

Use lower-level solutions and constraint multipliers in the penalty reformulation.

03

Update with first-order information

Analyze approximation and convergence under the stated convexity and regularity assumptions.

Dual variables carry constraint information

The primal-dual perspective attaches multipliers to the lower-level constraints. These variables help describe how the constrained optimum responds to the outer decision. BLOCC combines this information with a penalty formulation and first-order updates.

The theory has a specific regime

The paper assumes a strongly convex lower-level objective and constraints convex in the lower-level variable. It also requires feasible domains and constraint qualification. Under these conditions, the response and its dual description support the approximation and convergence analysis.

From a toy boundary to applications

The interactive example uses a bound that moves with the outer variable. The paper goes further with SVM hyperparameter selection and transportation design, including a network based on Seville. The connection is structural: an outer decision determines the lower-level problem that will actually be solved.

At an active constraint, the boundary is part of the response

If the follower’s optimum lies on a moving boundary, changing x affects the feasible choices as well as the objective. The constraint multiplier captures the contribution that an objective-only description would miss.

03Results

Test the model with constrained SVMs and networks

How to read this result

The analyzed lower-level objective is strongly convex in y, and the lower-level constraints are convex in y with the stated constraint qualification. Those conditions are part of the convergence guarantee.

04A closer look

Inside the method

min over x ∈ X of f(x, y*g(x)); y*g(x) ∈ argmin over Y(x) of g(x, y).

Y(x) = { y ∈ Y : c(x, y) ≤ 0 }. A constraint is coupled when it depends on x as well as y. The toy example below changes the bound y ≤ x and solves min (y − 2x)² over 0 ≤ y ≤ x.

x
The leader’s decision, which can change the follower’s constraints.
y*
The follower’s constrained optimal response.
c(x, y)
The lower-level inequality constraints.
λ*
Multipliers associated with those constraints.

The technical idea

The lower-level value changes through two routes

The derivative of v(x) contains an objective term ∇xg and a constraint term involving λ* and ∇xc. The multiplier-weighted term accounts for the movement of active constraints.

The toy example makes the multiplier tangible

For x > 0, the optimum y* = x lies on y ≤ x. The derivative of g with respect to y there is −2x, so stationarity gives multiplier λ* = 2x for that active upper bound. The lower bound is inactive.

The algorithm requires more than a toy KKT identity

BLOCC combines primal-dual information with a penalty approach. Its approximation and convergence analysis uses strong convexity in y, convex lower-level constraints, feasible domains, smoothness, and LICQ; the schematic only explains why constraint information matters.

Assumptions and guarantee

The penalty reformulation approximates lower-level optimality with a quantified error. The analysis uses strong convexity in y, convex constraints in y, nonempty feasible domains, Lipschitz regularity, and LICQ. See Assumptions 1–4 and the approximation and convergence theorems in Section 3.

How this connects to the other papers

The EUSIPCO 2025 paper sharpens the smoothness analysis of this penalty framework. The efficient-penalty preprint develops the broader analysis and the flatness-based update extension.
